translations.answer: AMP trains a discriminator on unstructured motion clips to produce a style reward and combines it with a task reward, reducing per-skill handcrafted imitation objectives. Its capability remains limited by data coverage, task definition, mode collapse, and the simulation-to-real gap; it is not a pipeline that turns any video into a deployable robot skill.
translations.applicability.assumptions.0: Motion data covers the required style and relevant state transitions.
translations.applicability.assumptions.1: Discriminator collapse, reward exploitation, and policy learning are monitored separately.
translations.applicability.controllers.0: Adversarial motion prior with a reinforcement-learning policy.
translations.applicability.environments.0: Physics-based character simulation tasks reported in the paper.
translations.applicability.robots.0: Simulated characters; not evidence from a physical humanoid.
translations.confidence_rationale: Multi-task experiments, ablations, and the pinned official implementation support the adversarial style-reward mechanism. Mode collapse, a paper/code formula difference, and simulation-only evidence bound the conclusion.
translations.evidence.0.locator: Figures 2–10, Tables 1–2, Sections 4–6, and the appendix.
translations.evidence.0.note: Defines adversarial style reward, task composition, motion data, and multi-skill experiments, and discusses mode collapse.
translations.evidence.0.title: AMP: Adversarial Motion Priors for Stylized Physics-Based Character Control
translations.title: Can AMP generate any usable skill automatically from motion clips alone?
